To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
children of refugees who have persistently high PTSD are more likely to have emotional and behavioural problems, and this is especially the case when both parents have persistently high symptoms.

children of refugees who have persistently high PTSD are at risk of having emotional and social difficulties and that the presence of both parents with persistentially high PTSD is more detrimental to child psychosocial functioning than when only one parent has persistently high PTSD.

children of recent Australian humanitarian entrants with persistently high levels of PTSD symptoms had higher levels of psychosocial difficulties than did children whose parents had lower levels of PTSD symptoms.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mental health of refugees and their families, and in particular with the impact of trauma on the mental health and adjustment of refugees.
the psychosocial wellbeing of children of humanitarian migrants, and how this may be affected by their parents’ experiences of traumatic stress.
the impact of parental PTSD on the psychosocial wellbeing of children.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of either a mother or a father with persistently high levels of post-traumatic stress disorder symptoms is associated with poorer child psychosocial functioning.

parental posttraumatic stress symptoms are associated with child emotional difficulties, and that the presence of persistently high PTSD in both parents is more strongly related to child emotional difficulties than when PTSD is present in just one parent.

the presence of either parent with persistently high levels of PTSD symptoms is associated with children having greater emotional difficulties than children whose parents do not have persistently high levels, but the impact on other domains of psychosocial adjustment is unclear.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

children of refugees who have parents with persistently severe PTSD symptoms are at greater risk of having emotional difficulties and poorer psychosocial adjustment than children whose parents do not have PTSD symptoms.
the presence of parental PTSD symptoms is associated with poorer child adjustment, but this association is stronger for children whose mothers have persistently high PTSD.
the presence of either a single or both parents with persistent PTSD symptoms is associated with greater emotional difficulties and overall psychosocial maladjustment in children.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is important to consider both parents' symptoms of PTSD when assessing the impact of parental mental health on children.
it is important to consider the impact of PTSD in parents on the psychosocial functioning of children, particularly when both parents have high levels of PTSD symptoms.
it is not just the presence or absence of parental PTSD symptoms that matter.
